text: [[drought|सूखा]] एक लंबा दौर है, जिसमें किसी जगह आम तौर पर जितनी बारिश या बर्फ़ गिरती है, उससे बहुत कम गिरती है। यह दबे पाँव आता है। पहले मिट्टी सूखती है। फिर फ़सलें मुरझाती हैं, नदियाँ सिकुड़ती हैं, झीलें नीचे उतरती हैं और कुएँ खाली होने लगते हैं। बाढ़ या तूफ़ान से अलग, कोई ठीक-ठीक नहीं बता सकता कि सूखा किस दिन शुरू हुआ।

इसकी मुख्य वजह मौसम के पैटर्न का खिसकना है। बारिश वाले बादल कहीं और चले जाते हैं, या बरसात का मौसम देर से आता है और जल्दी चला जाता है। गर्मी हालत और बिगाड़ देती है, क्योंकि गर्म हवा मिट्टी और पौधों से और भी ज़्यादा पानी [[evaporation|भाप बनाकर]] खींच लेती है।

sec.t:
भारत को साल की ज़्यादातर बारिश [[@monsoon|मानसून]] के चार महीनों में मिलती है। अगर ये बारिशें कमज़ोर रहीं, तो अगले साल तक दूसरा मौका नहीं मिलता। इसीलिए कमज़ोर मानसून किसानों, शहरों और सरकारों, सबकी एक साथ नींद उड़ा देता है।

1965 और 1966 में लगातार दो कमज़ोर मानसूनों ने भारत में खाने की भारी कमी कर दी। इस झटके ने देश को ज़्यादा पैदावार वाले नए बीजों, ज़्यादा [[irrigation|सिंचाई]] और खाद की ओर धकेला। इस बदलाव को बाद में [[@green-revolution|हरित क्रांति]] कहा गया।

दूर प्रशांत महासागर में गर्म पानी का एक हिस्सा, जिसे [[@el-nino|एल नीनो]] कहते हैं, अक्सर भारतीय मानसून को कमज़ोर कर देता है। हर बार नहीं करता, और यही एक वजह है कि पूर्वानुमान लगाना मुश्किल है।

{{story:millets}}

हमारे पैरों के नीचे बारिश का पानी चट्टानों और मिट्टी की दरारों में रिसकर जमा हो जाता है। इस जमा पानी को [[@groundwater|भूजल]] कहते हैं, और कुएँ इसी तक पहुँचते हैं। भारत दुनिया के किसी भी देश से ज़्यादा भूजल इस्तेमाल करता है। सूखे सालों में किसान और गहरा खोदते हैं और और ज़ोर से पंप चलाते हैं।

2016 में कई साल की कमज़ोर बारिश के बाद महाराष्ट्र के लातूर शहर में लगभग पानी ही नहीं बचा। टैंकर डिब्बों वाली एक ख़ास ट्रेन सैकड़ों किलोमीटर दूर से लाखों लीटर पानी शहर तक लाई। भूजल तभी भरता है जब बारिश का पानी वापस रिसकर नीचे जाए, और इसमें सालों लग सकते हैं।

बड़े शहर भी सुरक्षित नहीं हैं। 2018 में दक्षिण अफ़्रीका का केप टाउन उस दिन के बहुत करीब पहुँच गया, जिसे अधिकारियों ने "डे ज़ीरो" कहा था, यानी जिस दिन नल बंद कर दिए जाते। लोगों ने पानी का इस्तेमाल घटाकर हर आदमी लगभग 50 लीटर रोज़ कर दिया, जितना मोटे तौर पर एक छोटे शॉवर में लगता है, या कहो चार-पाँच बाल्टी। बारिश समय पर लौट आई और नल कभी सूखे नहीं।

जब कोई रिकॉर्ड नहीं रखता था, उस ज़माने के सूखों का हमें कैसे पता चलता है? पेड़ उन्हें याद रखते हैं। हर साल पेड़ नई लकड़ी का एक छल्ला जोड़ता है, गीले सालों में चौड़ा और सूखे सालों में पतला। बहुत पुराने पेड़ों और प्राचीन शहतीरों के छल्लों को आपस में मिलाकर वैज्ञानिकों ने सैकड़ों, बल्कि हज़ारों साल पुराने सूखों का पता लगाया है।

1930 के दशक में [[@usa-dust-bowl|अमेरिका के ग्रेट प्लेन्स में सालों तक सूखा पड़ा]]। किसानों ने गहरी जड़ों वाली उस घास को जोत डाला था, जो कभी मिट्टी को थामे रखती थी। बारिश रुकी तो सूखी ऊपरी मिट्टी बस उड़ गई। 14 अप्रैल 1935 को, जिसे ब्लैक संडे कहा जाता है, धूल के एक तूफ़ान ने कई राज्यों में दिन को रात बना दिया।

यह दौर डस्ट बाउल के नाम से जाना गया। लाखों लोग अपने खेत छोड़कर चले गए। बाद में अमेरिकी सरकार ने किसानों को हवा रोकने के लिए पेड़ लगाने और ऐसे तरीकों से जुताई करने के पैसे दिए, जिनसे मिट्टी अपनी जगह टिकी रहे।

लोगों ने हमेशा से सूखे दिनों के लिए बारिश का पानी बचाने के होशियार तरीके खोजे हैं। गुजरात और राजस्थान की [[@stepwells|बावड़ियों]] में लोग कई मंज़िल नीचे उतरकर पानी तक पहुँचते थे। आज भारत के बहुत-से शहर नई इमारतों से कहते हैं कि वे छतों से बारिश का पानी जमा करें।

फ़सलें भी मायने रखती हैं। बाजरा और रागी जैसे [[@millets|मोटे अनाज]] धान से कहीं कम पानी में उग जाते हैं। वैज्ञानिकों को उम्मीद है कि [[@climate-change|जलवायु परिवर्तन]] से कुछ इलाकों में सूखे ज़्यादा बार पड़ेंगे, इसलिए हर बूँद का हम कैसे इस्तेमाल करते हैं, यह और भी अहम हो जाएगा।

text: गड़गड़ाहट बिजली की आवाज़ है। बिजली की एक कड़क सेकंड के बहुत ही छोटे हिस्से में अपने आसपास की हवा को लगभग 30,000 °C तक तपा देती है। हवा इतनी तेज़ी से फैलती है कि किसी धमाके की तरह एक झटके वाली लहर बनकर बाहर धकेलती है। यही लहर तुम्हारे कानों तक गड़गड़ाहट बनकर पहुँचती है।

यह गरजती और लुढ़कती-सी इसलिए है, क्योंकि बिजली की लकीर लंबी होती है, अक्सर कई किलोमीटर। पास वाले सिरे की आवाज़ पहले पहुँचती है, और दूर वाले सिरे की कुछ सेकंड बाद। पहाड़ियों, इमारतों और बादलों से टकराकर लौटती [[@echoes|गूँज]] इस शोर को और खींच देती है।

sec.t:
[[@lightning|बिजली]] बिजली की एक विशाल चिंगारी है, उस छोटे झटके का बहुत बड़ा रूप जो तुम्हें कभी-कभी [[@static-electricity|स्थिर विद्युत]] से लगता है। जिस रास्ते से वह गुज़रती है, वह बस कुछ सेंटीमीटर चौड़ा होता है, पर उसमें बहने वाली [[current|धारा]] बेहिसाब होती है।

लगभग एक सेकंड के दस लाखवें हिस्से में उस रास्ते की हवा [[@sun-what|सूरज]] की सतह से कई गुना गर्म हो जाती है। गर्म हवा ठंडी हवा से ज़्यादा जगह घेरती है, और इस हवा के पास आराम से रास्ता छोड़ने का समय ही नहीं होता। वह बाहर की ओर फट पड़ती है और आसपास की हवा को दबा देती है। [[pressure|दबाव]] की यह लहर हर दिशा में [[@sound-travel|आवाज़]] बनकर फैल जाती है।

अगर बिजली बहुत पास गिरे, तो तेज़ कड़क या ज़ोरदार धमाका सुनाई देता है, क्योंकि लकीर के सबसे पास वाले हिस्से की आवाज़ एक साथ पहुँचती है। दूर से आवाज़ लंबा सफ़र तय करती है और कई चीज़ों से टकराकर लौटती है। पतली, ऊँची आवाज़ें फीकी पड़ जाती हैं और पीछे रह जाती है भारी, लुढ़कती गड़गड़ाहट।

लकीर का आकार भी मायने रखता है। बिजली टेढ़ी-मेढ़ी चलती है और शाखाओं में बँटती है। हर मोड़ से आवाज़ थोड़ी अलग दूरी से तुम तक आती है, इसलिए गड़गड़ाहट धमाकों की एक लंबी कतार बनकर पहुँचती है, जो आपस में घुलकर एक लंबी गरज बन जाती है।

गड़गड़ाहट आम तौर पर लगभग 15 किलोमीटर दूर तक सुनाई देती है, और बिजली भी तूफ़ान से इतनी दूर तक गिर सकती है। अमेरिका की राष्ट्रीय मौसम सेवा का एक सीधा नियम है: "बादल गरजें, तो अंदर चलो।" अगर तुम्हें गड़गड़ाहट सुनाई दे रही है, तो तुम इतने पास हो कि बिजली तुम पर गिर सकती है।

सबसे सुरक्षित जगहें हैं पक्की इमारत के अंदर या धातु की छत वाली कार में। तूफ़ान में पेड़, खुले मैदान और पानी सबसे ख़तरनाक जगहें हैं। भारत में बिजली ख़ासकर [[@monsoon|मानसून]] से पहले के हफ़्तों में और मानसून के दौरान बहुत गिरती है, और [[@imd|भारतीय मौसम विज्ञान विभाग]] तूफ़ान की आशंका होने पर चेतावनी भेजता है।

इतिहास के ज़्यादातर समय किसी को पता नहीं था कि गड़गड़ाहट क्यों होती है, इसलिए लोगों ने कहानियों से इसे समझाया। वेदों में देवताओं के राजा इंद्र वज्र नाम का अस्त्र चलाकर बारिश छुड़ाते हैं। [[@norse-myths|नॉर्स कथाओं]] में कहा जाता था कि थॉर का हथौड़ा गड़गड़ाहट पैदा करता है। यूनानी कहानियों में ज़्यूस बिजलियाँ फेंकते थे।

लगभग 2,000 साल पहले रोम के कवि ल्यूक्रेटियस ने सुझाया था कि शायद गड़गड़ाहट बादलों के टकराने से होती है। यह विचार बहुत लंबे समय तक चलता रहा। 1700 और 1800 के दशकों में वैज्ञानिकों ने दिखाया कि बिजली असल में विद्युत है, और गड़गड़ाहट उसी से पैदा होती है।

कभी-कभी गर्मी की रात में दूर क्षितिज पर बिजली टिमटिमाती दिखती है, पर कोई गड़गड़ाहट सुनाई नहीं देती। लोग इसे "गर्मी की बिजली" कहते हैं, पर यह किसी इतने दूर के तूफ़ान की आम बिजली ही है, जिसकी आवाज़ तुम तक पहुँच नहीं पाती। लंबी दूरी पर आवाज़ की [[vibration|तरंगें]] हवा में फीकी पड़ती हैं और मुड़ जाती हैं, इसलिए रोशनी तो आ जाती है पर आवाज़ नहीं। तुम्हारे [[@ears-hear|कान]] उसे पकड़ ही नहीं पाते।

text: Samudrayaan is India's plan to send people deep into the ocean. "Samudra" means ocean and "yaan" means vehicle. The mission is building a submersible, a small deep-diving craft, called Matsya-6000, after the fish avatar of Vishnu. It is designed to carry three people down to 6,000 metres below the surface of the Indian Ocean.

The mission is part of India's Deep Ocean Mission, run by the Ministry of Earth Sciences. The craft is being built by the National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT) in [[@chennai|Chennai]], with help from ISRO, the space agency behind [[@chandrayaan|Chandrayaan]]. As of 2026, the first crewed dive to full depth was aimed at about 2027.

st.prompt: Why is the crew cabin of Matsya-6000 shaped like a ball?

options.t: A sphere spreads the water's push evenly, so no spot is weaker than another
A ball can roll along the sea floor
It is the easiest shape to fit inside a ship

st.reveal: Deep water presses in from every side. A sphere shares that push equally across its whole surface, with no flat walls or corners to buckle. That's why nearly every deep-diving crewed submersible uses a ball for its crew.

sec.t:
Six kilometres down, the sea floor is cold, dark and mostly unexplored. Scientists want to study the animals living there, the shape of the sea bed and hot springs called [[@deep-sea-vents|vents]], where life feeds on chemicals instead of sunlight.

There is also something valuable lying on the floor of the Central Indian Ocean: potato-sized lumps called polymetallic nodules. They contain metals such as manganese, nickel, cobalt and copper, used in batteries and electronics. India has had permission since 1987 to explore a large patch of sea floor there. Some scientists warn that mining could harm deep-sea life, so studying it carefully first matters.

A submersible has to sink, hover and come back up. Matsya-6000 does this by changing its [[buoyancy|buoyancy]], how strongly water pushes it upward. It carries heavy weights to help it sink. At the bottom, it uses thrusters to move around. To return, it drops weights and floats back up to its mother ship.

The craft must also be found again in the open ocean. Like [[@submarines|submarines]], it uses sound signals underwater, since radio waves don't travel far through seawater.

India has tested the mission slowly, much like ISRO tests rockets before letting people fly on [[@gaganyaan|Gaganyaan]]. In 2021, an uncrewed steel sphere was lowered to about 6,000 metres to test equipment. In early 2025, Matsya-6000 completed wet tests in a harbour in Tamil Nadu, with crew inside. Shallow sea trials, to about 500 metres, were planned next.

In August 2025, two Indians trained by diving in the French submersible Nautile in the Atlantic. NIOT scientist Raju Ramesh reached about 4,025 metres, and retired Navy commander Jatinder Pal Singh reached about 5,002 metres, the deepest any Indian had gone.

Only a handful of countries have built crewed submersibles that can reach 6,000 metres or more, among them the USA, France, Russia, Japan and China. If Matsya-6000 succeeds, India will join them.

The sea covers about 70% of our planet, but as of 2024 only around a quarter of the sea floor had been [[@ocean-floor-maps|mapped]] in detail. Every dive will help fill in those blank spaces, and may reveal creatures nobody has ever seen in the [[@ocean-depths-life|deep sea]].

text: Pangolins are the only [[mammal|mammals]] covered in large hard scales. They are shy, slow, eat ants and termites, and live in parts of Asia and Africa. They are also hunted and smuggled more than any other wild mammal. Conservation groups estimate that over a million were taken from the wild between 2000 and 2013, and tonnes of their scales are still seized every year.

There are two main reasons. People in some countries eat pangolin meat as an expensive luxury, and their scales are used in some traditional medicines, especially in East Asia. Because a pangolin defends itself by rolling into a ball, a poacher can simply pick it up. All eight [[species|species]] are now protected by an international ban on trade.

st.prompt: What does a frightened pangolin do?

options.t: It rolls up into a tight scaly ball
It sprays a stinking liquid like a skunk
It climbs the nearest tree at top speed

st.reveal: A pangolin curls into a ball with its soft belly and face hidden inside. The overlapping scales are tough enough to stop most predators. Sadly, that makes it easy for poachers to simply pick one up.

sec.t:
Pangolins have no teeth. They rip open ant nests and [[@termite-mounds|termite mounds]] with strong front claws, then lick up the insects with a long, sticky tongue. In the giant pangolin, the tongue can reach about 40 cm, longer than the head and body together in smaller species. It is anchored near the pelvis and stored in a pouch in the chest.

Small stones and sand in the stomach help grind food. Scientists estimate that a single pangolin can eat tens of millions of insects a year, which makes them free pest control for farmers and forests.

India has two species. The Indian pangolin lives across much of the country, from the Western Ghats to dry forests in central India. The Chinese pangolin lives in the Himalayan foothills and the northeast.

Both are protected under India's Wildlife Protection Act, at the highest level, the same as tigers. Even so, Indian forest officials regularly catch smugglers carrying live pangolins or bags of scales towards borders. Many of them are rescued and returned to the wild.

In 2016, countries meeting under CITES, the [[treaty|treaty]] that controls wildlife trade, voted to ban all international commercial trade in all eight species. The ban came into force in 2017. In 2019, officials in Singapore seized more than 25 tonnes of pangolin scales in two shipments in one week, taken from tens of thousands of animals.

In 2020, China raised the protection level for its native pangolins and removed their scales from its official list of traditional medicines. Conservationists hope demand will fall, but smuggling continues.

Pangolins breed slowly. A mother usually has one baby a year, and the baby rides on her tail, clinging to her scales. Losing even a few adults from an area can take years to recover from.

They are also hard to keep in zoos, because they need special diets and get stressed easily. That means saving them in the wild is the only real option. World Pangolin Day, held on the third Saturday of February, spreads the word. And the creatures they eat, the [[@ants-world|ants]] and termites, have their own hidden superpowers.

text: [[compost|Compost]] is what you get when plant and food waste rots in a controlled way. [[bacteria|Bacteria]] and fungi, too small to see, feed on peels, leaves and scraps. As they eat, they break them down into a dark, crumbly material that smells like a forest floor. Worms, beetles and other small creatures help by chewing and mixing.

The finished compost is full of [[humus|humus]], the rich part of soil that holds water and feeds plants. Gardeners and farmers mix it into the ground to grow healthier crops. Making compost also keeps waste out of rubbish dumps, where rotting food gives off a gas that warms the planet.

st.reveal: Without air, different microbes take over and make smelly gases. Adding dry leaves or shredded paper and turning the heap lets air back in. A healthy heap smells like a forest floor.

Poke small air holes, cover the top with cloth and keep it in the shade. Mark the level and check it each week as the pile shrinks and darkens.

A healthy compost heap smells earthy, like soil after rain. A bad smell is a sign that something is off, usually too much wet food waste and too little air or dry material.

sec.t:
A compost heap needs two kinds of ingredients. "Greens" are wet, fresh things like vegetable peels, fruit skins, tea leaves and grass clippings. They are rich in nitrogen, which the [[microbe|microbes]] use to build their bodies. "Browns" are dry things like fallen leaves, straw, twigs and shredded paper. They are rich in carbon, which the microbes burn for energy.

Many gardeners use about two or three buckets of browns for every bucket of greens. Too many greens and the heap turns slimy and smelly. Too many browns and it hardly rots at all. Meat, dairy and oily food are usually kept out of home heaps, because they attract rats and flies.

Not all compost is hot. In vermicomposting, special worms called red wigglers do most of the work. They live in a box or bin, eat kitchen scraps and leave behind dark, rich droppings called castings.

Vermicomposting is popular in India, on farms and in city flats, because it works in a small space and doesn't smell when done right. Common garden [[@earthworms|earthworms]] do a similar job outdoors, pulling dead leaves underground and mixing them into the soil.

In the 1920s, a British plant scientist named Albert Howard was working at an agricultural institute in Indore, in central India. He watched how local farmers used animal dung and crop waste, and worked out a careful system of layering, watering and turning heaps. He called it the Indore method.

Howard wrote books about it, and his ideas spread to farms and gardens across Europe and America. Many gardeners who build compost heaps today are following steps first tested in Indian fields about a hundred years ago.

Food and garden waste make up a big share of what households throw away. In a landfill, buried under other rubbish without air, it rots slowly and gives off methane, a gas that traps far more heat than [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]]. In a compost heap with plenty of air, the same waste turns into something useful instead.

Some cities collect wet waste separately and compost it in big plants. Others encourage families to compost at home. Leftovers can also be turned into cooking gas in a [[@biogas|biogas]] plant. Either way, a banana peel that goes back into the [[@soil-made|soil]] helps grow the next banana, which is a neat way to cut down on [[@food-waste|food waste]].

text: Recycling turns old things into raw materials for new things. First, used items are collected, from bins, from homes, or from the street. Then they are sorted by material: paper, cardboard, glass, metals and different kinds of plastic. Sorting is the most important step, because mixed materials are hard to use.

Next, each material is cleaned and broken down. Paper is soaked into a mushy pulp. Glass is crushed into small pieces. Metals are shredded and melted. Plastic is chopped into flakes and melted into small pellets. Factories then use these materials to make new products, from fresh cardboard boxes to cans, bottles, park benches and even clothes.
Recycling saves raw materials and usually a lot of energy, and it keeps rubbish out of landfills and the sea.

st.reveal: Steel contains iron, which is magnetic, so big magnets lift steel cans off the moving belts. Aluminium isn't magnetic, so plants use a different trick, a spinning magnetic field that pushes aluminium cans off the belt as if they were kicked.

sec.t:
In many American and European cities, mixed recycling goes to big sorting plants. Conveyor belts carry it past a series of machines. Spinning screens let small things fall through and carry flat paper away. [[@magnets-how|Magnets]] lift out steel cans. A spinning magnetic field flings [[@aluminium|aluminium cans]] off the belt. Light [[sensor|sensors]] spot different plastics, and puffs of air blow each one into its own bin.

People still check the belts by hand, pulling out things that shouldn't be there, like plastic bags that tangle the machines. Dirty items cause trouble too. A jar still full of pickle or a greasy pizza box can spoil a whole bale of clean paper, which is why rinsing things before recycling them helps.

Aluminium is the star of recycling. Remelting it uses about 95% less energy than making new aluminium from rock, and it can be recycled endlessly. Steel and [[@glass-made|glass]] can also be recycled over and over without wearing out.

[[@paper-made|Paper]] is different. Each time it is pulped, its fibres get shorter, so after about five to seven rounds they are too short to hold together. New fibres from wood must be mixed in. Very short fibres often end up in egg cartons or newsprint, which don't need to be strong.

[[@plastic-made|Plastic]] is the hardest. There are many kinds, and they can't easily be mixed. Plastic usually gets weaker each time it is melted, so a bottle often comes back as something less demanding, such as carpet, fleece jackets or stuffing for pillows. Researchers estimated in 2017 that only about 9% of all plastic ever made had been recycled.

Recycling still uses energy, water and trucks. That's why many people say "reduce, reuse, recycle", in that order. The best rubbish is the rubbish you never make.

Carrying a cloth bag, refilling a steel [[@water-bottle|water bottle]] and repairing broken things often do more good than recycling. A steel tiffin carried to school for years saves hundreds of plastic boxes. Recycling is the last step, for things that can't be avoided or reused. Many Indian homes already do this without calling it anything special: glass jars become pickle jars, old saris become quilts, and newspapers end up at the kabadiwala.

text: लोग मुखौटे इसलिए बनाते हैं ताकि कोई और बन सकें, इंसान या कुछ और। मुखौटा पहनो और तुम देवता, राक्षस, जानवर, [[ancestor|पूर्वज]] या नायक बन सकते हो। हर बसे हुए महाद्वीप पर मुखौटे नाच, रंगमंच, धार्मिक [[ritual|अनुष्ठानों]], त्योहारों, अंतिम संस्कारों, युद्ध और खेलों में दिखते हैं।

ये बचाते भी हैं। सर्जन, वेल्डर, दमकलकर्मी और हॉकी के गोलकीपर, सब मुखौटे पहनते हैं। कुछ मुखौटे मृतकों का सम्मान करते हैं, जैसे तूतनख़ामून का सोने का मुखौटा। कुछ बस मज़े के लिए होते हैं, जैसे [[@halloween|हैलोवीन]] पर बच्चों के भेस। मुखौटा इंसानी चेहरे को, जिसे हम दूसरों में सबसे पहले पढ़ते हैं, किसी नई चीज़ में बदल देता है।

sec.t:
2014 में यरूशलम के इज़राइल म्यूज़ियम ने लगभग 9,000 साल पुराने पत्थर के मुखौटों का एक समूह दिखाया, जो जूडिया की पहाड़ियों और रेगिस्तान में मिले थे। उनमें आँखों के छेद, मुँह, और किनारों पर छोटे छेद हैं, शायद उन्हें बाँधने या टाँगने के लिए।

कोई ठीक-ठीक नहीं जानता कि वे किसलिए थे। बहुत-से जानकार मानते हैं कि वे पूर्वजों के प्रतीक थे, और शायद अनुष्ठानों में पहने जाते थे या घरों में रखे जाते थे। वे उस दौर के हैं जब लोग पहली बार खेती वाले गाँवों में बसने लगे थे।

पूर्वी भारत में [[@art-chhau|छऊ]] नर्तक रामायण, महाभारत और स्थानीय किंवदंतियों की कहानियाँ पेश करते हैं। पश्चिम बंगाल की पुरुलिया शैली में नर्तक पंखों, मोतियों और चमकीली पन्नी के मुकुटों वाले बड़े, रंगीन मुखौटे पहनकर उछलते और घूमते हैं। झारखंड की सरायकेला शैली में मुखौटे छोटे और सौम्य होते हैं। ओडिशा के मयूरभंज की तीसरी शैली में मुखौटे होते ही नहीं।

असम के नदी-द्वीप [[@majuli|माजुली]] पर सत्र कहलाने वाले वैष्णव [[monastery|मठों]] के भिक्षु बाँस, मिट्टी और कपड़े से मुखौटे बनाते हैं। कुछ तो पूरे शरीर को ढकने वाले विशाल मुखौटे होते हैं, जो कृष्ण और राम के नाटकों में काम आते हैं। कर्नाटक में [[@yakshagana|यक्षगान]] कलाकार ज़्यादातर इसकी जगह गाढ़ा मेकअप करते हैं, यानी खुद चेहरे पर रँगा हुआ मुखौटा।

जापान में 1300 के दशक में शुरू हुए नो रंगमंच के कलाकार लकड़ी के मुखौटे पहनते हैं। हर मुखौटा इतनी बारीकी से तराशा जाता है कि ज़रा-सा झुकाने पर उसका भाव बदल जाता है। प्राचीन यूनान के [[@theatre|रंगमंच]] में कलाकार चौड़े मुँह वाले मुखौटे पहनते थे, जो उनकी आवाज़ को हज़ारों लोगों तक पहुँचाने में मदद करते थे।

इटली का वेनिस एक मशहूर कार्निवल मनाता है, जिसमें लोग सजे-धजे मुखौटे पहनते हैं। भूटान में भिक्षु त्सेचु कहलाने वाले त्योहारों पर मुखौटे पहनकर नाचते हैं। पूरे पश्चिमी और मध्य अफ़्रीका में लकड़ी के मुखौटे आत्माओं और पूर्वजों के सम्मान में होने वाले अनुष्ठानों का हिस्सा हैं, और पिकासो जैसे कलाकारों ने इनसे प्रेरणा ली।

1959 में कनाडा के गोलकीपर ज़ाक प्लांत के चेहरे पर आइस हॉकी की पक (चपटी गेंद) आकर लगी। वे मुखौटा पहनकर खेल में लौटे, और एनएचएल, यानी उत्तर अमेरिका की बड़ी आइस हॉकी लीग, में नियमित रूप से मुखौटा पहनने वाले पहले गोलकीपर बन गए। जल्दी ही दूसरों ने भी ऐसा ही किया। आज खेलों में मुखौटे और वाइज़र उतने ही आम हैं जितने [[@helmets|हेलमेट]]।

1800 के दशक के आखिर में डॉक्टरों ने कीटाणुओं को रोकने के लिए सर्जिकल मास्क पहनने शुरू किए। 2020 से कोविड-19 [[pandemic|महामारी]] के दौरान अरबों लोगों ने रोज़ मास्क पहने। वैज्ञानिकों ने पाया कि मास्क से [[@emotions|भावनाएँ]] पढ़ना थोड़ा कठिन हो जाता है, क्योंकि हम मुँह से बहुत कुछ पढ़ते हैं, हालाँकि बहुत-सी बातें आँखें भी कह देती हैं।

text: People live in an enormous variety of homes, from apartments in [[@skyscrapers|skyscrapers]] to tents, houseboats, mud huts, snow houses and caves. A home's shape and materials usually depend on the local [[climate|climate]], the materials close at hand, how much money people have, and whether they stay in one place or move around.

In hot places, homes often have thick walls, small windows and shady courtyards. In cold places, they hold in warmth. In places that flood, they may stand on stilts. In crowded cities, people live stacked on top of each other in tall buildings.

st.reveal: Packed snow is full of trapped air, which makes it a good insulator. Body heat and a small lamp can keep the inside of an igloo tens of degrees warmer than the air outside.

myth: Inuit people lived in igloos all year round.

Igloos were mostly used as winter shelters, especially while travelling or hunting. Many Inuit lived in houses of stone, whalebone and turf in winter and in skin tents in summer. Today most live in modern houses.

sec.t:
Inuit in [[@arctic|the Arctic]] built igloos from blocks of packed snow, mainly as shelters during winter hunting trips. Snow is full of trapped air, so it keeps warmth in. With people and a small oil lamp inside, an igloo can be around freezing while the air outside is −40 °C.

In [[@mongolia|Mongolia]], many herding families live in round felt tents called *gers*, also known as [[@life-homes-world|yurts]]. They are warm in fierce winters and can be taken apart and loaded onto animals or trucks when the family moves to new pasture.

About 800 years ago, the Ancestral Puebloan people built villages of stone rooms tucked into cliffs at Mesa Verde, in what is now Colorado, USA. The overhanging rock sheltered them from sun and snow.

In Coober Pedy, Australia, many people live in "dugouts" carved into hillsides. Underground, the temperature stays comfortable all year while summer air outside can top 40 °C. In Matmata, Tunisia, families dug homes around deep pits in the ground.

Today more than half the world's people live in cities, many in apartments. In [[@mumbai|Mumbai]], some families live in chawls, older buildings with rows of single rooms opening onto a shared corridor. Others live in high-rise towers. In the United States, many families live in separate houses with their own gardens, especially in suburbs.

Millions of people around the world live in informal settlements, built by residents themselves without official permission. They are often crowded and lack clean water or drains, but they are also full of families and small businesses.

New homes keep appearing too, from houses made of recycled shipping containers to apartments built by 3D printers.

A home is more than walls and a roof. It is where families eat, sleep, celebrate and store their memories. Who lives inside also varies, from one person to large joint families, as you can read in [[@families-world|families around the world]]. [[@jobs-architect|Architects]] today are borrowing ideas from traditional homes, like thick earth walls and shady courtyards, to build houses that stay cool without much electricity.

text: Prices go up when there is more money chasing goods than there are goods to buy, or when it costs more to make and move things. This general rise in prices over time is called inflation.

A little inflation is normal and even expected. If prices rise by 4% in a year, something that cost ₹100 last year costs about ₹104 now. The money in your pocket buys a bit less. India's central bank, the Reserve Bank of India, tries to keep inflation near 4%, and anywhere between 2% and 6% counts as on target. America's Federal Reserve aims for 2%. Prices that rise far faster than that can hurt families, especially poorer ones, who spend most of their money on food and fuel.

st.prompt: If prices rise by 6% a year, roughly how long until they double?

options.t: About 12 years
About 50 years
About 3 years

st.reveal: A handy trick called the rule of 72 says you divide 72 by the yearly rise. 72 divided by 6 is 12, so prices would roughly double in 12 years. At 2% a year, it takes about 36 years.

myth: Inflation means everything gets more expensive at the same rate.
Inflation is an average. In the same year, vegetables might jump in price while phones or televisions get cheaper. Your own family's costs may rise faster or slower than the official figure.

sec.t:
The first cause is demand. When people have more money to spend and shops can't keep up, sellers raise prices. A good harvest year has the opposite effect: plenty of vegetables, lower prices.

The second is cost. If fuel becomes expensive, everything carried by truck costs more, from tomatoes to cement. A poor [[monsoon|monsoon]] can push up food prices across India.

The third is money itself. If a government prints large amounts of new money without more goods being made, each rupee or dollar is worth less. That is why central banks, not politicians, usually control how much money is created.

{{story:great-depression}}

Very fast inflation is called hyperinflation. In Germany in 1923, after the [[@world-war-one|First World War]], the government printed huge amounts of money. [[@exponents|Prices doubled every few days]]. By the end of the year, a loaf of bread cost billions of marks. Families saw their life savings vanish.

In Zimbabwe, prices rose so fast in 2008 that early the next year the country printed a note worth 100 trillion Zimbabwean dollars. Soon after, it gave up its own [[currency|currency]] and used foreign money instead. These cases are rare, but they show why governments take inflation seriously.

Every month, government statisticians check the prices of a long list of things a typical household buys: rice, milk, [[@cooking-gas|cooking gas]], rent, school fees, haircuts, bus fares. This "basket" gives a consumer price index. Comparing it with the same month a year earlier gives the inflation rate as a [[@percentages|percentage]].

The basket is an [[@averages|average]], so it won't match every family. A household that eats lots of vegetables feels a tomato price spike more than one that doesn't. In India, the National Statistics Office publishes these figures every month. In the USA, the Bureau of Labor Statistics does the same job.

Sometimes prices rise in disguise. A company keeps the price of a biscuit packet the same but quietly puts fewer biscuits inside. People have nicknamed this shrinkflation, and it is one reason to check the weight printed on a packet.

The main tool is the interest rate. When inflation is too high, the central bank raises the rate at which banks borrow. Loans become more expensive, so people and businesses borrow and spend less, and price rises slow down.

After the COVID-19 [[pandemic|pandemic]], prices jumped around the world as supply chains broke down and fuel became expensive. US inflation hit about 9% in June 2022, its highest in about four decades. Central banks raised interest rates sharply, and inflation gradually came down. It showed how much a few [[@percentages|percentage]] points can change what ends up in a family's shopping bag, and how the [[@money-interest-loans|interest on loans]] is tied to the price of bread.

text: In a [[@democracy-what|democracy]], people choose their leaders by voting. In India, every citizen aged 18 or over can vote, and each vote counts the same, whether the voter is a farmer or a film star.

In 2024, nearly 97 crore people were registered to vote, more than the whole population of Europe. About 64 crore actually voted, over 44 days in seven phases. The [[@election-commission|Election Commission]] tries to make sure nobody has to travel more than about 2 km to vote, so it set up over 10 lakh polling stations.
Your vote is secret. Nobody else needs to know who you chose.

d.try: Hold a secret ballot in your class on something simple, like the next class story. Everyone writes a choice on a slip, folds it and drops it in a box, and two people count the slips in front of everyone. Then try the same vote by show of hands. Talk about whether anyone voted differently when others could see.
myth: One vote never makes a difference.
In the 2008 Rajasthan assembly election, C.P. Joshi lost his seat in Nathdwara by a single vote. Close results happen more often than people think, especially in local elections.

sec.t:
The Election Commission of India [[@elections-india|organises elections]] and makes sure they're free and fair. The [[@constitution|Constitution]] set it up in 1950, and it is independent of the government.

Before an election, it updates the voter list, announces the dates and sets rules, called the Model Code of Conduct, that all parties must follow. Crores of teachers, officials and police officers are drafted in as election staff. They carry voting machines by boat, on foot, on elephants and by helicopter.

Voters press a button next to a candidate's name and symbol on an electronic voting machine, used across India since 2004. A printer beside it shows a paper slip for a few seconds, so voters can check their choice. These printers have been used at every booth since 2019.

A mark of special ink on the left forefinger shows you've voted, so nobody votes twice. It contains silver nitrate, which darkens in light and lasts for days. It is made by a company in Mysuru, Karnataka. Since 2013, voters can also choose NOTA, "none of the above".

The rule about reaching voters is taken seriously. Tashigang in [[@himachal|Himachal Pradesh]], over 4,600 m up, has one of the highest polling stations in the world.

For years, officials walked into Gir forest in Gujarat to set up a booth for a single voter, a priest at a temple deep in lion country. In the [[@andaman|Andaman Islands]] and the north-east, booths are reached by boat and long treks.

All the votes from every phase are counted on a single day, weeks after the first ones were cast. Machines are kept sealed and guarded in strong rooms until then. Counting starts in the morning, and by evening the country usually knows the result, which TV channels follow seat by seat.

People elect Members of [[@parliament-india|Parliament]] to the Lok Sabha, members of state assemblies, and local [[@panchayat|panchayats]] and municipal councils. A third of seats in panchayats and municipalities are reserved for women.

Some elections have been won by just a handful of votes. In 2008, a candidate in Rajasthan lost an assembly seat by one vote. That's why making voting easy for everyone matters, from a voter in a big city to one in a forest.

text: Data science is the job of turning a big pile of numbers and facts into answers. A data scientist collects information, cleans out the mistakes, looks for patterns, and then explains what those patterns mean.

It mixes three things: maths (especially [[@statistics-lies|statistics]]), computer skills for handling millions of records, and plain good sense about which questions are worth asking. Weather forecasts, film suggestions on streaming apps and the route your maps app picks all come from people and programs doing data science.

sec.t:
In 1854, cholera swept through Soho in London and killed hundreds of people in a few days. Most doctors then believed the disease spread through bad air. A doctor named John Snow had a different idea.

He walked the streets, asked families where they got their water, and marked each death on a map. The marks bunched up around one public pump on Broad Street. Snow convinced local officials to remove the pump's handle. The outbreak was already fading by then, but his map became famous evidence that cholera travels through dirty water.

That is the heart of data science: collect carefully, look for a pattern, then test it.

In 1931, the scientist Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis founded the Indian Statistical Institute in Kolkata. He worked out how to learn about a whole country by carefully questioning a fair sample of people, instead of everyone. His methods helped set up India's National Sample Survey in 1950, which still measures things like what families spend and how many people have jobs. His birthday, 29 June, is now celebrated as National Statistics Day in India.

The same idea powers modern [[@surveys|surveys]]: ask the right few thousand people, and you can say something sensible about crores.

Today the piles of data are enormous. Every tap on a phone, every UPI payment and every ball bowled in the IPL can be recorded. Data scientists write programs, often called [[@algorithms|algorithms]], that sift through these records far faster than any person could.

Hospitals use data to spot which patients may need extra care. Cricket and baseball teams use it to choose where fielders should stand. Farmers use rainfall data to decide when to sow. Much of modern [[@ai-what|artificial intelligence]] is built by training computer programs on huge collections of data.

Data can fool people too. If ice-cream sales and drowning cases both rise in summer, it does not mean ice cream causes drowning. Hot weather drives both. Data scientists call this the difference between correlation (two things moving together) and causation (one thing making the other happen).

Bad data causes trouble as well. If a survey only asks people who own smartphones, it misses everyone who doesn't. Much of the real work is checking, cleaning and doubting the numbers before believing what they seem to say.

text: Money in a bank grows because the bank pays you interest. Banks lend your money to other people and businesses and share some of what they earn with you. If the interest is added to your savings, then next year you earn interest on the interest too. That's called compound interest.

At first the growth is slow. Then it speeds up, because the pile keeps getting bigger and the interest is a [[percentage|percentage]] of the whole pile. Given enough years, a small amount can grow into a surprisingly large one, without you adding a single rupee.

st.prompt: You put ₹1,000 in a bank that pays 10% interest a year, added on each year. Roughly how long until you have ₹2,000?

options.t: About 7 years
Exactly 10 years
About 20 years

st.reveal: Simple interest would take 10 years, adding ₹100 each year. With compound interest, each year's interest also earns interest, so the money doubles in just over 7 years. The rule of 72 gives 72 ÷ 10 = 7.2.

d.try: Make a doubling chart. Start with 1 rupee and double it every day for 30 days, writing each number on a calendar. Guess first how much you'll have on day 30, then check. The answer, more than 50 crore, surprises almost everyone.
myth: Einstein said compound interest is the most powerful force in the universe.
This quote is all over the internet, but there is no record that Einstein ever said it. It began appearing decades after his death. The maths is real, even if the quote isn't.

sec.t:
Say you save ₹1,000 at 10% interest a year. With simple interest, you get ₹100 every year, always worked out on the first ₹1,000. After 10 years you have ₹2,000.

With compound interest, year one gives ₹100, so you have ₹1,100. Year two gives 10% of ₹1,100, which is ₹110. Year three gives ₹121. The amount added grows every year. After 10 years you have about ₹2,594. After 30 years, simple interest gives you ₹4,000, but compound interest gives you over ₹17,000.

That's the strange power of [[@exponents|exponents]]. The number gets multiplied again and again, not just added to.

[[@benjamin-franklin|Benjamin Franklin]], the American inventor and statesman, wanted to show what patience could do. When he died in 1790, his will left £1,000 each to the cities of Boston and Philadelphia. The money was to be lent to young workers, and most of it left untouched to grow for 200 years.

Franklin worked out that it might grow to millions. Things didn't go perfectly. Philadelphia's fund was managed less carefully and grew more slowly. Still, by 1990 Boston's fund was worth about $4.5 million and Philadelphia's about $2 million. A technical college in Boston, now called the Benjamin Franklin Cummings Institute of Technology, was founded in 1908 partly with money from that gift.

sec.h: The other side of the coin
sec.t:
Compound interest also works against you. If you borrow money, on a credit card for example, the interest can compound too. A debt left unpaid can double in a few years. That's why adults warn about borrowing more than you can pay back.

Some loans in history became famous traps. Moneylenders in villages charged such high compound interest that farmers could stay in debt for their whole lives. Many Indian reformers, and later India's banks and [[cooperative|cooperatives]], worked to give farmers fairer loans.

The biggest ingredient in compound interest is not the amount you start with. It's time. Someone who saves a little from age 15 can end up with more than someone who saves twice as much from 35. The early money simply has longer to double and double again.

Doubling gets out of hand fast. An old Indian legend tells of a king asked to pay one grain of rice on the first square of a chessboard, then two, then four. By the 64th square, the rice would bury the whole kingdom, and the [[@puzzle-chessboard-rice|chessboard puzzle]] shows exactly how.

text: Aadhaar is a 12-digit number given to people who live in India. Each number belongs to just one person, for life. The word "aadhaar" means foundation or support in Hindi.

When you enrol, your name, date of birth, address and photo are recorded, along with all ten [[@fingerprints|fingerprints]] and [[@biometrics|scans of both irises]], the coloured rings in your eyes. These body measurements are called [[biometric|biometrics]]. Later, [[@fingerprint-sensors|a fingerprint or iris scan]] can check that you are really the person linked to that number. The system is run by the Unique Identification Authority of India, known as UIDAI.

st.prompt: Who can get an Aadhaar number?

options.t: Anyone living in India for long enough, including some foreigners
Only Indian citizens
Only adults over 18

st.reveal: Aadhaar is open to residents of India, including foreign nationals who have lived in India for 182 days or more in the past year. Children can have one too. That is why Aadhaar is a proof of identity, not a proof of citizenship.

src: Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI), About Aadhaar.

d.try: Make a fingerprint card. Rub a soft pencil on a scrap of paper until it is dark, press your fingertip on it, then press a piece of clear sticky tape onto your finger and stick the tape on white paper. Compare your print with a family member's. Look for loops, whorls and arches.
myth: An Aadhaar card proves that you are an Indian citizen.
Aadhaar proves who you are, not your nationality. Residents of India, including some foreign nationals, can get one. Citizenship is shown by other documents, such as a passport.
facts: name, birth date, address, photo, 10 fingerprints and both irises

sec.t:
Before Aadhaar, many people, especially the poor, had no official papers at all. Without proof of who you are, it was hard to open a bank account, get a SIM card or receive government help like subsidised grain.

The idea was to give everyone a single, simple way to prove their identity. Government money for [[@pensions-old-age|pensions]] and scholarships could then go straight into a person's bank account, linked to their Aadhaar. This helped millions open bank accounts, and it made payment systems like [[@upi-payments|UPI]] easier to spread.

Children can have Aadhaar too. Under the age of five, a child gets a blue "Baal Aadhaar" card based on a photo and a parent's details, with no fingerprints taken, because small children's fingerprints are still changing.

At five and again at fifteen, the child's fingerprints and iris scans must be updated. Your face and hands change a lot as you grow, and the system needs a fresh record to recognise you. Schools sometimes hold special camps so that students can get these updates done in one go.

Not everyone was comfortable with one giant database. Critics worried that linking Aadhaar to bank accounts, phones and travel could let someone track a person's whole life, and that a data leak could expose millions. Others pointed out that fingerprint machines sometimes fail for elderly people or manual workers with worn fingertips, who then struggled to get rations. To get around that, many offices also accept a one-time password sent to a registered phone, or a scan of the eyes.

Supporters argued that Aadhaar reduced fraud, saved government money and helped people who had been left out.

The [[@supreme-courts|Supreme Court]] stepped in. In 2017 it ruled that [[@privacy|privacy]] is a fundamental right of every Indian. In 2018 it said Aadhaar itself was allowed, but it could not be made compulsory for things like school admission, opening a bank account or getting a mobile connection. It is still required for some things, such as filing income tax and many government benefits.

The United States has a different system: a nine-digit Social Security number, started in the 1930s, with no fingerprints attached.

text: Radio in India began with amateurs. In 1923 a radio club in Bombay (now Mumbai) began broadcasting, and other clubs followed in Calcutta and Madras. In 1927 a private company, the Indian Broadcasting Company, opened stations in Bombay and Calcutta. It soon ran short of money, and the British government took over.

In 1936 the government service was renamed All India Radio. After independence it grew into one of the largest radio networks in the world, carrying news, music, farming advice and plays in many languages. Since 1957 it has also been officially called Akashvani, a Sanskrit-based word meaning "voice from the sky".

options.t: Tuned in to Radio Ceylon from Sri Lanka instead
Stopped listening to film music
Built their own radio stations at home

st.reveal: Radio Ceylon played the latest film hits, and its countdown show Binaca Geetmala became hugely popular across India. In 1957 All India Radio answered with Vividh Bharati, a channel full of film songs.

Radio still reaches places where phones and TV struggle, like remote villages, fishing boats and farms. All India Radio broadcasts in dozens of languages, and many people listen through mobile apps too.

sec.t:
Radio sends sound using [[@radio-waves|radio waves]], invisible waves that travel at the speed of light. A station turns voices and music into a changing radio signal and sends it from a tall tower. A radio set picks up the signal and turns it back into sound.

In the 1930s a radio set was expensive, so many villages had a single community set in a square or panchayat office. People gathered around it for news, the way families later gathered around one TV.

On the night of 14 August 1947, All India Radio carried Jawaharlal Nehru's "Tryst with Destiny" speech as India became independent at midnight. Families across the country heard it live.

Radio also became a teacher. From the 1960s, All India Radio ran farm programmes in local languages, telling farmers about new seeds, [[fertiliser|fertilisers]] and the weather, which helped spread the Green Revolution. It carried cricket too. Ball-by-ball commentary in English and Hindi let fans follow Test matches long before most homes had a television. In 2014 the prime minister began a monthly radio talk, Mann Ki Baat, on the same network.

Three months after independence, on 12 November 1947, Mahatma Gandhi made his only visit to a radio studio, in Delhi, to speak to [[refugee|refugees]] from Partition. That day is still marked as Public Service Broadcasting Day.

sec.h: Film songs and a rival station
sec.t:
In the 1950s, the government decided that Hindi [[@film-songs|film songs]] were too lightweight and cut them back on All India Radio. Listeners switched to Radio Ceylon, broadcasting from Sri Lanka. Its weekly countdown show, Binaca Geetmala, hosted by Ameen Sayani, became a national habit.

All India Radio got the message. In 1957 it launched Vividh Bharati, a channel packed with film music, requests and [[@radio-shows|radio shows]]. It is still on air. Private FM stations were allowed from the early 2000s, and big cities now have dozens of channels playing music and chat. News on radio is still mostly left to All India Radio. The name Akashvani has its own story. It was first used in 1936 by M.V. Gopalaswamy, a professor in Mysore who started a small station at his home. Today the network reaches almost every corner of India, and a farmer in a field and a commuter on the Delhi Metro can hear the same news bulletin at the same moment.

text: Virtual reality, or VR, puts you inside a world made by a computer. You wear a headset that covers your eyes, and wherever you turn your head, the picture changes as if you were really there. The real room disappears.

Augmented reality, or AR, keeps the real world in view and adds computer images on top. A phone game that shows a cartoon creature sitting on your real table is AR. So is a filter that puts puppy ears on your head in a video. *Augmented* means added to.

st.prompt: Why do some people feel sick in VR even though they are sitting still?

options.t: Their eyes see movement but their inner ear feels none
The headset is too heavy
The screen gives off a special gas

st.reveal: Your balance comes partly from your inner ear, which senses real movement. When your eyes say you are racing downhill but your inner ear says you are sitting on a sofa, the brain gets confused, and some people feel queasy. Faster, smoother screens help.

d.try: Hold one finger up at arm's length and look at it, closing one eye, then the other. Your finger seems to jump sideways. Each eye sees a slightly different view, and your brain combines them into depth. A VR headset uses exactly this trick, showing each eye its own picture.
myth: VR and AR are just new kinds of video games.
Games are a big part of it, but doctors use VR to practise surgery, pilots and astronauts train in it, and engineers use AR to see how machines fit together before building them.

sec.t:
You have two eyes a few centimetres apart, so each sees the world from a slightly different angle. Your brain combines the two views to judge depth. [[@3d-glasses|3D glasses]] at the cinema use this trick, and so does a VR headset.

Inside the headset are two small screens, or one split in half, with a lens in front of each eye. Each eye gets its own picture, drawn from a slightly different position. The [[@lenses-glasses|lenses]] make the screens look large and far away.

People have loved 3D pictures for a long time. In 1838 the British scientist Charles Wheatstone described the stereoscope, a viewer that showed each eye a slightly different drawing. In 1939 the View-Master toy put 3D photos on cardboard reels, and children have collected them ever since.

In 1968 the American computer scientist Ivan Sutherland built a headset that drew simple wire-frame shapes over the real room. It was so heavy it hung from a mechanical arm attached to the ceiling. Cheap, light headsets only arrived in the 2010s, when phone screens and sensors became small and powerful.

Most people first meet AR on a phone. The camera shows the room, and software spots flat surfaces like floors and tables, then places 3D objects on them so they stay put as you walk around. In July 2016 Pokémon Go sent millions of people outdoors to catch creatures that appeared on their screens in parks and streets.

Shops use AR to let you see how a sofa would look in your living room. Some cars show directions on the windscreen. Museums use it to bring old ruins back to life on a screen.

[[@robots-surgery|Surgeons practise operations]] in VR before touching a patient. Pilots have trained in simulators for decades, and VR makes that cheaper. [[@future-schools|Students]] can "visit" the inside of a cell or the surface of Mars.

Headsets can still be heavy, hot and tiring after a while. Many makers set a minimum age of 10 to 13 for their headsets and suggest regular breaks, because young eyes and brains are still developing. It's a good idea to check the age guidance with a parent before trying one.

text: Frederick Douglass was born enslaved in Maryland, in the United States, around 1818. He secretly learned to read, escaped to freedom in 1838 and became one of the most famous Americans of his time. He spoke and wrote against slavery, published his own newspaper and advised presidents.

His [[autobiography|autobiography]], published in 1845, showed thousands of readers what slavery was really like. He also fought for women's right to vote, for equal rights after the Civil War and for an end to unfair treatment of Black Americans. He died in 1895.

st.prompt: How did Frederick Douglass escape from slavery in 1838?

options.t: He took a train and a boat north, dressed as a sailor, with borrowed papers
He walked for months through forests at night
He was freed by his owner in a will

st.reveal: Douglass borrowed the papers of a free Black sailor and dressed in a sailor's clothes. He travelled by train and steamboat from Baltimore and reached New York in less than a day.

d.try: Douglass said learning to read was his "pathway from slavery to freedom". Write a short letter to someone you admire, explaining why reading or writing matters to you. You can send it, or keep it as a reminder.
myth: Abraham Lincoln and Frederick Douglass always agreed with each other.

Douglass criticised Lincoln strongly at first for moving too slowly against slavery. They met three times at the White House, and Douglass came to respect him, but he never stopped pushing for faster change.

sec.t:
Douglass was born Frederick Bailey. He never knew his exact birthday. As a small child he was separated from his mother, who worked on a plantation miles away.

At about eight, he was sent to work for a family in Baltimore. The wife began teaching him the alphabet until her husband stopped her, saying reading would make a slave unfit for slavery. Douglass realised that reading was exactly the key he needed. He traded bread with poor white boys in the street for reading lessons, and taught himself to write by copying letters on walls and fences.

He bought a book of speeches with money he earned shining shoes. Reading about freedom made him determined to win his own.

In 1841, Douglass spoke at an anti-slavery meeting. People were stunned by his power. He began touring as a speaker. Some listeners refused to believe such a brilliant man had ever been enslaved.

To prove it, he wrote *Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass*, published in 1845. It named real people and places, which put him in danger of recapture. He went to Britain and Ireland for nearly two years. Supporters there raised money to buy his freedom legally.

Back home, he started a newspaper, *The North Star*, in 1847. In 1852 he gave a famous speech asking, "What to the slave is the Fourth of July?" It pointed out that Americans celebrated freedom while millions were still enslaved.

During the [[@us-civil-war|Civil War]], Douglass pushed [[@abraham-lincoln|Abraham Lincoln]] to free enslaved people and let Black men fight. When Black soldiers were finally allowed to join the Union army, two of his sons enlisted. He met Lincoln at the White House three times. Douglass had often criticised him for moving too slowly, but he came to respect him.

After the war, slavery was abolished. Douglass held government jobs, including US Marshal for the District of Columbia and US minister to Haiti.

In 1848, Douglass was one of the few men at the Seneca Falls Convention in New York, the first big meeting for women's rights in the US. He spoke in favour of women's right to vote. He worked with campaigners like [[@susan-b-anthony|Susan B. Anthony]], though they disagreed sharply after the war over whether Black men should get the vote before women.

He died at his home in Washington, DC, on 20 February 1895, after speaking at a women's rights meeting that day. The house, called Cedar Hill, is now a museum run by the National Park Service.

text: Meriwether Lewis and William Clark led an [[expedition|expedition]] across the western part of North America from 1804 to 1806. President [[@thomas-jefferson|Thomas Jefferson]] sent them after the United States bought a vast area called Louisiana from France in 1803, roughly doubling the country's size.

Their team, called the Corps of Discovery, travelled by boat, on foot and on horseback from near St. Louis to the Pacific coast and back. They mapped rivers, recorded hundreds of plants and animals new to science, and met dozens of Native nations. They did not find the easy water route Jefferson hoped for, but they showed Americans what lay to the west.

The Rocky Mountains

st.reveal: The rivers did not link up. Between the Missouri and the rivers flowing to the Pacific stood the Rocky Mountains, far wider and higher than anyone in the East expected. The team had to cross them on foot and horseback, nearly starving on the way.

d.try: Keep an explorer's journal for one week. Each day, sketch one plant, insect or bird you see near home or school, describe it in words, and note the weather. Lewis and Clark did exactly this, and their notes are still read by scientists.
myth: Lewis and Clark explored empty, unknown land.
Every place they went was already home to Native nations, who knew it well. The expedition survived because many of those nations gave food, horses, maps and advice.

sec.t:
In 1803 France sold Louisiana to the United States for 15 million dollars. It stretched from the [[@mississippi|Mississippi]] to the Rocky Mountains. France had lost interest partly because of the [[@haitian-revolution|revolution in Haiti]], which cost [[@napoleon|Napoleon]] his richest colony.

Few Americans had seen this land. Jefferson wanted to know what was there, and whether a boat could travel by river to the Pacific Ocean. He chose Lewis, his private secretary, who then asked his old army friend Clark to share the command.

In August 1805 the expedition reached the Shoshone. By an astonishing chance, their chief, Cameahwait, turned out to be Sacagawea's brother, whom she had not seen since she was kidnapped as a child. The Shoshone traded horses the team badly needed.

Crossing the Bitterroot Mountains was the hardest part. Snow fell, game was scarce, and the men ate candles and some of their horses. When they stumbled out, hungry and ill, the Nez Perce people fed them and looked after their horses. In November 1805 they finally saw the Pacific. Clark wrote in his journal, "Ocian in view! O! the joy."

The expedition included York, a man enslaved by Clark. He hunted, scouted and voted with the others on where to spend the winter. Yet after they returned, Clark refused for years to free him. Lewis also brought his big black Newfoundland dog, Seaman, who caught squirrels for the cooking pot and guarded the camp at night.

The team returned to St. Louis in September 1806, long after many people had given them up for dead. Their journals described about 178 plants and 122 animals unknown to Western science, including the grizzly bear and the prairie dog. Clark's [[@maps-history|maps]] were used for decades.

In spring 1805 the team even sent a live prairie dog back east by boat. It made the journey of thousands of kilometres and arrived alive at Jefferson's home, the White House, along with skins, bones and seeds.

For Native nations, the journey marked the start of something harder. Settlers, traders and soldiers soon followed the route, and many nations lost their lands. In 2000 the United States put Sacagawea on a one-dollar coin.

text: Nalanda was a huge Buddhist [[monastery|monastery]] and centre of learning in [[@bihar-history|Bihar]], about 90 km southeast of Patna. It was founded in the 5th century CE, during the [[@gupta-golden-age|Gupta age]], and flourished for around 700 years.

Monks and students lived there, studying Buddhist [[philosophy|philosophy]] along with logic, [[@grammar-why|grammar]], medicine and astronomy. Scholars came from [[@china-today|China]], [[@ancient-korea|Korea]], Tibet and Southeast Asia. Because it had teachers, students, lecture halls and a library, it is often called one of the world's first universities, long before Oxford or Bologna. Around 1200 CE it was attacked and destroyed. Its red-brick ruins are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

This story is very popular, but no record from the time describes it. It first appears in much later writings. The destruction was real, but the six-month fire may be a legend.

sec.t:
In the 7th century, a Chinese monk named Xuanzang set out to find the original Buddhist texts. He crossed deserts and mountains along the [[@silk-road|Silk Road]] and spent several years studying at Nalanda.

His account and his [[biography|biography]] describe tall towers, pools with blue lotuses and teachers known across Asia. He says about 10,000 people lived there. Xuanzang took hundreds of texts back to China and spent the rest of his life translating them. Much of what we know about Nalanda comes from him and from another Chinese monk, Yijing, who came a few decades later.

Tibetan tradition says Nalanda's library was spread over three buildings with poetic names: Sea of Jewels, Ocean of Jewels and Delighter of Jewels. Books were copied by hand on palm leaves and birch bark.

Some Nalanda [[manuscript|manuscripts]] survived because monks carried them to Tibet and [[@nepal|Nepal]]. Today a few are kept in museums far from Bihar. Each one was copied by a scribe working slowly, one letter at a time.

[[@paper-invention|Paper]] was not yet in common use in India, so a single long text could fill a stack of leaves as thick as a brick. Losing a library like this meant losing books that might exist nowhere else. That is why scholars treasure every leaf that escaped.

By the 12th century, Buddhism had weakened in India. Around 1200 CE, soldiers led by Bakhtiyar Khalji attacked monasteries in Bihar. A history written a few decades later describes a monastery being destroyed and its monks killed. Scholars still discuss whether that account refers to Nalanda or to a nearby monastery, but Nalanda was ruined around this time.

Over the centuries, the site disappeared under earth and grass. The Archaeological Survey of India began careful excavations in 1915 and uncovered monasteries, temples and [[stupa|stupas]].

In 2016, UNESCO listed the ruins as a World Heritage Site. You can walk among the thick brick walls and peer into the tiny rooms where students once slept.

Not far away, near Rajgir, a new Nalanda University opened in 2014, with help from several Asian countries. It moved into a new campus in 2024. The old name is back, along with its idea of students from many lands learning together.

text: The Appalachians are a long chain of mountains running down the eastern side of North America, from Newfoundland in Canada to Alabama in the southern USA. They are rounded and covered with forests, and the highest peak, Mount Mitchell, is just over 2,000 metres. That's lower than [[@himachal|Shimla]].

They look gentle because they are very old. The Appalachians were pushed up in stages between about 480 and 270 million years ago, long before [[@dino-age-span|the first dinosaurs]]. They were probably once as tall as the Alps, and perhaps taller. Since then, hundreds of millions of years of rain, frost and rivers have worn them down to their roots.

st.prompt: The Great Smoky Mountains are wrapped in a blue-grey haze on most summer days. Where does it come from?

options.t: Natural gases given off by the forest, mixed with water vapour
Smoke from old coal mines burning underground
Steam rising from hot springs

st.reveal: Trees and other plants release natural chemicals into the air, especially on warm days. These, together with water vapour, scatter blue light and make the famous haze. Pollution from far away can make it thicker and greyer.

n.certNote: Geologists agree the Appalachians were once much taller than today. How tall is uncertain, because the rock that would tell us has worn away, so estimates range from Alps-sized to Himalaya-sized.

myth: The Smoky Mountains got their name from smoke from fires.
The smoke is a natural haze. The Cherokee name for the area is often translated as "place of blue smoke", long before modern fires or factories.

sec.h: Born in a crash of continents

sec.t:
In 1921, a forester named Benton MacKaye proposed a walking trail along the whole ridge, so that city people could escape into the wild. Volunteers cleared paths and built shelters, and the Appalachian Trail was finished in 1937. It runs about 3,500 kilometres from Springer Mountain in Georgia to Mount Katahdin in Maine.

Each year, a few thousand people try to walk all of it in one go. It takes most of them five to seven months, and many give up along the way. Hikers follow white paint marks on trees and rocks, about the size of a dollar bill.

Because the southern Appalachians escaped the ice sheets of the last ice age, plants and animals had a long, steady time to [[evolve|evolve]]. The region has more kinds of salamander than anywhere else on Earth. Some breathe through their skin and have no lungs at all.

In early summer, at Elkmont in Great Smoky Mountains National Park, thousands of male [[@fireflies|fireflies]] of one [[species|species]] flash at the same moment, then go dark together. The effect is so popular that the park runs a lottery for places to watch. The Great Smoky Mountains is the most visited national park in the USA, with over 12 million visits in recent years.

The Cherokee and other Native nations lived in the southern Appalachians for thousands of years. In 1838 and 1839 the US government forced most of the Cherokee to leave for land far to the west. Thousands died on the journey, now called the Trail of Tears.

Settlers from Scotland, Ireland, England and Germany brought fiddles and ballads to the mountain valleys. African Americans brought the banjo, which has roots in West African instruments. Their music blended into old-time and bluegrass, two of the roots of [[@country-music|country music]].

The mountains also hold thick seams of [[@oil-coal|coal]], formed from swamps of giant plants about 300 million years ago. Coal mining gave the region jobs for more than a century, but also dangerous work and damaged hills.

text: Books get children reading when they are hard to put down. Exciting stories, characters children care about and worlds they want to return to all help. So does choice: children read more when they can pick books they like, not just ones set for school.

Series help a lot. Once you love a character, you want the next book, and each one makes the following one easier. Being read to, seeing adults read and having books close at hand, at home or in a [[@libraries|library]], all make reading a [[@habits|habit]].

Harry Potter showed all of this on a giant scale. Its seven books, published between 1997 and 2007, sold more than 600 million copies in over 80 languages. Many children who had never read a long book read all seven, some more than once.

st.prompt: According to reading researchers and librarians, which of these most often turns a child into a regular reader?

options.t: Being allowed to choose books they actually enjoy
Being made to read the longest books first
Only reading books set for school

st.reveal: Studies and surveys keep finding that choice matters. Children read more when they pick books themselves, whether that is fantasy, comics, sports stories or facts about sharks. Being read aloud to at home, even after learning to read, helps too.

sec.h: The boy who lived, and almost wasn't printed

sec.t:
By the later books, publication days became events. Children dressed as wizards and queued outside bookshops at midnight. *Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows*, the final book, sold millions of copies in its first 24 hours in 2007.

The books grew longer as the series went on. The fifth, *Order of the Phoenix*, runs to more than 750 pages in its British edition. Yet many children who had found 100 pages hard now raced through it. Because readers had grown up alongside Harry, each book felt like meeting an old friend.

In India, the books were translated into Hindi and several other Indian languages, and English editions sold widely in cities. Rowling filled the books with invented words, from "Quidditch" to "Muggle", and "muggle" was later added to the Oxford English Dictionary. Readers who learned those words were also picking up long, tricky ones like "ominous" and "incantation" along the way.

sec.h: Did it really make more readers?
sec.t:
Many parents and teachers believe it did, and surveys for publishers found many young fans said the books made them enjoy reading. But big studies of reading habits, such as one by America's National Endowment for the Arts in 2007, found that teenagers overall were reading for fun less than before.

Both can be true. A book can turn millions of children into readers while, at the same time, other things like screens compete for everyone's free hours. Researchers still argue about how big the "Harry Potter effect" was.

sec.h: Other books that did the same
sec.t:
Harry Potter was not the first series to do this. Enid Blyton's Famous Five and Secret Seven hooked generations of children in Britain and India. Nancy Drew mysteries did it in the USA. In India, *[[@amar-chitra-katha|Amar Chitra Katha]]* and [[@tinkle|Tinkle]] comics got many children reading before they ever opened a novel.

More recently, series like *Diary of a Wimpy Kid* and [[@percy-jackson|Percy Jackson]] have pulled in readers, especially those who said they didn't like books. What they share is simple. Children want to know what happens next.

text: Chaat is a family of savoury snacks from North India, sold at street stalls and eaten at all times of day. A typical plate mixes something crunchy, like fried papdi or puffed rice, with something soft, like boiled potatoes or chickpeas. Then come cool curd, a [[@tamarind|sweet tamarind chutney]], a sharp green chutney, crunchy sev and a sprinkle of tangy chaat masala.

The magic is in the contrast. Each bite is sweet, sour, salty, spicy, hot and cold, crunchy and soft. Your [[@tongue-taste|tongue]] and nose get many signals at once, which is part of why chaat is so hard to stop eating.

st.prompt: Kala namak, the black salt in chaat masala, smells a bit like boiled eggs. Why?

options.t: It contains sulphur compounds
It is made with egg shells
It is mixed with fish powder

st.reveal: Kala namak is a rock salt that's heated with other ingredients, which creates sulphur compounds. Sulphur is also what gives boiled eggs their smell. Despite the name, the salt is usually pinkish-grey when ground.

d.try: Make a mini chaat taste test with an adult. Put a few boiled chickpeas on a plate and add a different topping to each little group: a drop of lemon, a pinch of sugar, a pinch of salt, a pinch of chaat masala. Taste each, then mix them all. Notice how the combined spoonful tastes stronger than any one alone.
myth: Different parts of your tongue taste different flavours, with sweet at the tip and bitter at the back.
This "tongue map" is wrong. Taste buds all over the tongue can sense sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. Some areas may be slightly more sensitive, but every part tastes every flavour.

sec.t:
Chaat-wallahs, the cooks who make chaat, build each plate by hand in seconds. For papdi chaat, they crack crisp flour wafers onto a leaf plate, add potatoes and chickpeas, pour on whisked curd, then splash on two chutneys.

The sweet chutney is made from tamarind and [[@jaggery|jaggery]] or dates. The green one is coriander, mint and green chilli. On top go sev, pomegranate seeds, chopped onion, coriander leaves and a pinch of chaat masala. The whole thing is eaten quickly, before the papdi goes soggy.

Delhi and Uttar Pradesh have aloo tikki, crisp potato patties topped with chutneys and curd, and dahi bhalla, soft lentil dumplings soaked in curd. In Lucknow, cooks serve chaat in a crisp edible basket called a tokri.

Mumbai has its own chaat family. Bhel puri mixes puffed rice, sev, onion, potato and chutneys, and it's sold on the sands of Juhu and Chowpatty beaches. Sev puri tops flat puris with potato and chutneys. Ragda pattice pairs potato patties with a white pea curry.

Kolkata loves jhalmuri, puffed rice tossed with [[@mustard|mustard]] oil, onions and green chillies, and sold in paper cones.

Nobody knows exactly where chaat began. A popular story says it started in Delhi in the time of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, in the 1600s. Royal doctors supposedly advised people to eat spicy, tangy food to fight the effects of water from the Yamuna. There's no clear evidence for this tale.

What is clear is that chaat grew up on the streets of North Indian cities. Chandni Chowk in Old [[@delhi|Delhi]] has been famous for its chaat stalls for generations.

Because chaat is street food, many people worry about hygiene. Good stalls use clean water, fresh chutneys and cover their food. It's sensible to choose busy stalls where food doesn't sit around for long, and to ask an adult before trying somewhere new.

Chaat has also spread far beyond the street. You can find it at weddings, in restaurants and in Indian cafés in cities like London and New York. Some American restaurants now serve chaat dishes, introducing new eaters to the sweet-sour-crunchy mix that North Indian children have loved for generations.
